significance: State temple of Jayavarman VII, the empire's great Buddhist king — a forest of towers carved with over 200 colossal serene faces, compassion gazing to every horizon. Its outer galleries, uniquely, depict ordinary Khmer life — markets, cockfights, childbirth — beside the naval battle with the Chams that framed the king's rise.
story: The faces fuse Avalokiteshvara with Jayavarman himself — the bodhisattva-king watching all his people at once; stand anywhere in the Bayon and at least one face meets your eyes, the architectural claim that compassion has no blind spot.
